item.title: Law enforcement dismantle cocaine network from Ecuador to Europe
item.description: An international investigation supported by Europol and Eurojust has dismantled a criminal network suspected of importing cocaine into Europe from Ecuador and other Latin American countries. Investigators link the network to large quantities of seized cocaine, including a recent seizure of over 750 kilos in Antwerp, Belgium.

item.title: 354 dark web vendors and buyers arrested in Europol-coordinated global crackdown
item.description: Europol, in collaboration with law enforcement agencies from 14 countries across the globe, have successfully identified vendors and buyers from major dark marketplaces as part of Operation TorNado, a coordinated international effort targeting cybercrime, drug trafficking, and firearms offences. The operation, which spanned from May 2025 to October 2026, resulted in 354 arrests and hundreds of house searches worldwide.

item.title: Operation OPSON XV dismantles food fraud networks, seizing EUR 79 million in counterfeit products
item.description: Operation OPSON XV, which ran from December 2025 to May 2026, involved 57 countries across several continents. item.title: Five TEFAF robbery suspects added to EU Most Wanted
item.description: As of 29 October 2026, five new fugitives, four men and one woman, have been added to the EU Most Wanted list. According to the Limburg Public Prosecutor's Office (Openbaar Ministerie) and the Dutch Police (Politie), all five suspects are involved in the European Fine Art Fair (TEFAF) robbery that took place on 28 June 2022 in Maastricht, the Netherlands.

item.title: Investment scams with potential victims in at least 50 countries: over 100 servers seized

item.title: Palo Alto confirms Fragnesia exploitation against firewalls in PHP2Shell attacks
item.description:
Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers exploited Fragnesia, a Linux kernel flaw, to gain root on PAN-OS firewalls through the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, and has shipped fixes six months after the bug was patched in Linux.

The vulnerability allows a locally authenticated, low-privileged attacker to escalate privileges to root.

“Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” the company said in its November 25 security advisory. It added that all observed attacks targeted devices whose management interface “is exposed to the internet, a configuration our best practices advise against.”

Even so, the company labeled the bulletin “Informational” and gave it no CVSS score. Fixed builds span every supported PAN-OS branch from 10.2 to 12.2.

A second patch cycle in a month

For PAN-OS customers, these are the second set of hotfixes in a month. Between October 25 and October 29, Palo Alto released fixes for PHP2Shell, according to the timeline in its PHP2Shell advisory. PHP2Shell is the collective name for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical flaws in the PHP runtime behind the PAN-OS management web interface.

The company rated both flaws 9.2 on CVSS 4.0, and the advisory, which covers PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama, said, “active exploitation has been observed.”

The October builds do not include the kernel fix, which arrives in later releases listed in the new bulletin. Even for customers who have patched PHP2Shell, Palo Alto said in the bulletin that it “still recommend[s] upgrading to a fixed release at your next maintenance interval.”

Palo Alto is relaxed about the timing. “If you are running a fixed PAN-OS listed in the CVE-2026-109618 advisory, you are protected,” the bulletin said. “The only known way to exploit this vulnerability requires an attacker to first exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerability,” it added. For devices with management access restricted to trusted internal IP addresses, it advises upgrading “at your next maintenance interval.”

Duncan Brown, group vice president and global domain lead for worldwide security and trust at IDC, said that the approach is defensible when vulnerabilities are chained.

“It’s acceptable to apply one patch that effectively breaks the chain. Ideally, all vulnerabilities would be patched as early as possible, but in many cases this is not practical,” Brown said.

Rahul Karne, a senior digital forensics and incident response analyst, called patching PHP2Shell a reasonable short-term step, but said it blocks the known way in without fixing the bug.

“The key word is ‘known,’” Karne said. He pointed out that public exploit code for Fragnesia, including a Metasploit module, is available, and that any other code execution flaw on the device would make the kernel bug usable again.

From web shell to root

The chain has been public for almost a month. In late October, Dream Security researchers reported that attackers combined PHP2Shell with Fragnesia to compromise firewalls running vulnerable PAN-OS builds.

According to Dream, the attackers used PHP2Shell to run code as the web service account and then used the kernel flaw to become root. From there, they tunneled into internal networks and stole credentials, private keys, and network topology data.

The kernel bug itself is not new. William Bowling, a researcher at Zellic, disclosed Fragnesia on May 13 along with a proof-of-concept exploit and an upstream kernel patch, after finding it with the help of the company’s V12 AI auditing agent. Fedora shipped a fixed kernel the next day.

Karne said some delay is normal for appliance vendors that maintain custom kernels across many hardware models, but 195 days is too long when exploit code is public. Customers should hear whether they are affected within a week of such a disclosure and get a fix within about 30 days, he said.

“A firewall should not get security fixes more slowly than the servers it protects,” Karne said.

The firewall as a foothold

Palo Alto is not the only security vendor whose appliances were rooted this way. In November, Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers were hit after attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Gaia OS privilege escalation flaw to take over gateways and deploy a wiper.

Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said CISOs should treat the incident as a weakness in their trust model for security appliances, not merely a patching issue.

“A firewall running Linux, PHP and other third-party components must be assessed with the same rigor as any privileged, internet-facing server,” Daftary said. “Vendor labels such as ‘Informational’ should never override enterprise risk analysis when flaws can be chained to achieve root access.”

“If a device is exposed during the attack window, merely applying the hotfix does not establish trust,” she added. Teams should review administrative access, rotate credentials and certificates, hunt for persistence, and reimage the appliance from a known-good build when root compromise cannot be ruled out, she said. Asked why the kernel fix took six months to reach PAN-OS, and whether Panorama is affected, Palo Alto said it had “no further information to share beyond what is outlined in the advisory at this time.”

item.title: SAP security advisory – November 2025 monthly rollup (AV25-738) – Update 1
Switzerland Confirms AI-Assisted Cyberattacks Breached Critical Infrastructure Operators
item.description:
Attackers using AI agents have broken into computer systems at Swiss organizations in four of five confirmed attacks, the first such cases in the country, the country's cybersecurity agency said yesterday.

item.title: 1Password data breach included some customer info, internal source code
item.description:
1Password is reassuring customers that their password vaults are safe after the theft of both account records for a subset of its users and source code from its private repositories.

The company said it began investigating the incident on November 19, after it detected indications that an employee’s corporate GitHub account had been breached.

The attacker used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded what 1Password described as “administrative data” about a subset of users. This included customer names and email addresses, account and user IDs, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters, and “other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture.”

Tokens used in some emailed links to customers inviting them to accept provisioning invitations or account recovery were also stolen, although 1Password said that these tokens must be combined with an SSO sign-in or a six-digit confirmation code sent to the user’s registered email address before account access is granted. The company has notified affected customers and, to further secure authentication, has changed the confirmation code format from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters.

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and accessed the continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) system; while 1Password said that the source code contained no user secrets, infrastructure secrets in the CI/CD system may have been exposed. The company has triggered a rotation of all relevant credentials.

Vaults not affected

However, it emphasized, customers’ password vaults were not affected, nor were the keys that protect them. The company also pointed out that it does not store account passwords or secret keys; customers are the only ones who have keys to their vaults.

Account recovery keys and 1Password apps and browser extensions are also safe, it said.

Actions taken

1Password said that, in response to the breach, as well performing the credential rotation and lengthening of confirmation codes, it has disabled the compromised GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access created by the attacker. It also has tightened internal controls on GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoints and added new detections for attacks such as this.

Finally, it checked for internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise, and has brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate its efforts.

Recommendations for customers

In its post, 1Password warned customers to beware of phishing attacks in the wake of this incident and reminded them that it will never contact them to ask for account passwords or Secret Keys. “Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser,” it advised.

Fritz Jean-Louis, principal cybersecurity instructor at Infotech, also recommended that customers monitor for suspicious activity, particularly phishing attempts that exploit concerns about the breach, adding that security teams should pay close attention to unexpected account recovery requests and unusual account provisioning activity as well.

He noted that, although this is a serious breach of 1Password’s backend environment, it is somewhat mitigated by the fact that, according to the company, there is no evidence that customer password vaults were compromised.

“For organizations using the service, that distinction is important,” he said. “Some customer account information was affected, but the vaults containing passwords and secrets were not reported to have been accessed. Based on the information disclosed so far, I do not see a need for a blanket reset of passwords stored in those vaults solely because of this incident.”

This is also a good opportunity for organizations to review all of their identity and access monitoring, he added. “Organizations should verify that their security information and event management system is monitoring those activities and providing meaningful alerts,” he said. “Even where a third party handles that monitoring, it is worth checking that the right coverage is in place.”

item.title: Broadcom issues fixes for 23 new VMware flaws, three critical
item.description:
Broadcom on Tuesday reported almost two dozen new security vulnerabilities in VMware, adding to a lengthy list of fixes from this month alone.

The most serious of the flaws in the current advisory is a vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, CVE-2026-123903, assigned a CVSSv3 base score of 9.8 (Critical). “A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system,” it said. 

In a supplemental document accompanying the alert, Broadcom noted that because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing, the advisory comes just two days before the US Thanksgiving holiday, admitting, “this timing is not optimal.”

The company said that the advisory covers a total of 23 issues, seven of which are in vCenter: an authentication bypass and three denial-of-service issues in the VMware Directory Service, an arbitrary file write while processing certain archives, a local privilege escalation in a vpxd service script, and a security policy enforcement failure in the vSphere Distributed Switch (vDS).

Seven more are in ESX: a heap out-of-bounds write and a use-after-free in the I/O filter service, an out-of-bounds write in the Extensible Host Controller Interface (XHCI) USB controller, a stack-based buffer overflow in the VMkernel, a security bypass in the host configuration store, a signature verification bypass, and a denial of service in guest RPC.

The remaining flaws affect VMware Workstation, VMware Fusion, VMware Tools, and VMware Avi Load Balancer.

However, the company noted that the fixes delivered to address the flaws in last week’s advisory resolve some of the issues highlighted in the current batch.

“If you applied vCenter 8.0 U3m for VMSA-2026-0009, including on VCF 5.2.x, you do not need to update vCenter again, but vCenter 9.1.x needs the update in this advisory,” Broadcom said.

“ESX was not part of VMSA-2026-0009 and needs the update in this advisory. VMSA-2026-0009 also resolved issues in SDDC Manager, which this advisory does not update. If you have not applied the SDDC Manager update from VMSA-2026-0009, apply it separately. This advisory also includes a VMware Tools update. Updating vCenter and ESX does not update VMware Tools inside virtual machines, so plan that update separately.”

It added, “if you have a question about whether you are affected, it is likely that you are and should take action immediately.”

Difference of opinion on patching urgency

So is this a signal to interrupt the US Thanksgiving holiday to address the flaws? Opinions differ.

Tyler Reguly, Fortra’s associate director of security R&D, argued that although a 9.8 score is about as high as they get, the nature of the holes might not merit extreme scheduling. There are three vulnerabilities rated 9.8 in severity listed in the current batch, affecting VMware vCenter and ESX.

He pointed out, “neither of these [affected] systems should be present on your external interfaces, so the risk would need to be internal. That means we’re talking about an inside threat or a breach that is already underway. These are important vulnerabilities, so there’s no doubt about that, but they are not so important that anyone should interrupt their holiday weekend.”

Reguly suggested a strict interpretation of CISA guidance to support his contention that these patches may not merit emergency response. 

“If we take a look at CISA BOD-26-04 as our guidance on this, is the service publicly exposed? It shouldn’t be, so let’s say no. Is this vulnerability in the KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog]? No. Could it be automated? Unknown, so let’s assume yes for safety’s sake,” he said. “A result of No, No, and Yes translates to line 13 on the BOD-26-04 remediation timelines, which allows for 60 days to fix the issue.”

He observed that the recent onslaught of vulnerabilities has made us “a bit like Pavlov’s dog:” We’ve been conditioned to react every time we see CVSS 9.8.

“This is a dangerous and potentially harmful conditioning that we need to make every effort to break,” he said. “We need to remind ourselves that the severity of a vulnerability does not reflect risk to an organization, just as the bell did not represent food.”

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, disagreed.

He considered the current advisory, VMSA-2026-0011, to be “a big deal because it hits vCenter and ESX, the two systems that run every virtual machine, with flaws that need no password. Skip the patch, and one attacker can take down or take over every virtual machine you run. You are essentially toast. Patch now.”

Dickson noted that this batch of alerts contains multiple problematic security issues, which include authentication bypass in vCenter; permitting an attacker with network access to run code on the hypervisor itself; and another bug that lets an administrator inside a virtual machine on Workstation or Fusion run code on the host computer. “Let’s face it: AI loves to chain vulnerabilities,” he said.

He is also worried about the large number of VMware patches this month alone, especially those in vCenter. “The frequency of VMware’s vCenter flaws is a concern, as they keep landing in the same place,” he said. “The new flaw is distinct from last week’s. Distinct is not comforting. Three different holes in the same wall is a wall problem.”

He pointed out, “The directory service has become vCenter’s Achilles’ heel. This advisory adds three denial-of-service flaws in the same service for good measure.”
